thread.title: AT&T: Don't Celebrate This Dividend Hike - AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T)

author: Stone Fox Capital
title: AT&T: Don't Celebrate This Dividend Hike - AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T)
text:
Last week, AT&T ( T ) announced the annual tradition of hiking the dividend a minimal amount. The company ceremoniously highlighted this annual tradition, but investors shouldn't celebrate this dividend hike. My investment thesis remains bullish with the stock at $30, but these dividend hikes aren't the reason.
Image Source: AT&T website
Another 2% Hike On Friday, AT&T announced a 2% hike in the quarterly dividend to $0.51 from $0.50. The new dividend yield jumps to 6.8%.
The company had the following statement that highlights the historical problems of dividends:
Our healthy cash flows and strong outlook for 2019 give us the confidence to raise our dividend for the 35 th consecutive year . The dividend is an important way we provide value to our shareholders, and I’m proud that we are able to continue our history of annual increases .
Notice the emphasis is on raising the dividend for 35 consecutive years and a history of increases, not growing free cash flows or any metric reflective of actual financial health. Like most companies, AT&T is talking solely about the arbitrary decisions of management on what to distribute to shareholders.
The company has averaged a dividend growth rate of slightly above 3% over the last decade.
Source: Seeking Alpha dividends page
While investors claim to want steady dividend hikes, the market doesn't actually reward companies with such dividend paths. Over the last decade, AT&T has consistently hiked the dividend, but the yield has fluctuated wildly.
T Dividend data by YCharts The issue is that dividends have become an obligation. Value Line made the following statement about the attractiveness of dividends:
Moreover, consistent payouts underscore a company’s cash generation capabilities, while dividend increases demonstrate management’s confidence in the future.
The problem here is that this concept only works if management hikes annual dividends based on actual confidence in the business. The reality is that AT&T is managing the dividend hike to artificially attempt to influence investor confidence.
The dividend hike isn't based on actual results, hence the problem with the hikes turning into obligations. Even worse, AT&T is discussing selling prime assets like the 10% position in Hulu in order to meet the additional payout requirements of an annual $0.04 dividend hike on 7.28 billion shares.
Dividend Hike Problems AT&T is now boxed into the corner with these expected dividend hikes. The market is clearly telling the wireless and media giant that it would prefer the company pay down debt and the current 6.7% dividend yield was more than rewarding for shareholders. Otherwise, the amount of the dividend payout wasn't a restraining factor in people owning the stock.
The issue is the large debt load and the requirements of covering the massive dividend payout. At the Investor Day, AT&T recently announced the intent of reaching annual FCFs of $26 billion .
The problem here is that quarterly dividend payouts were $3.64 billion for a $14.5 billion annual dividend payout. A simple $0.01 quarterly hike adds an additional $73 million in quarterly payouts on 7.28 billion shares outstanding. The amount may not seem large, but the long-term impact adds up as follows:
2019: quarterly hike $0.01 = $73M 2020: quarterly hike $0.01, cumulative $0.02 = $146M 2021: quarterly hike $0.01, cumulative $0.03 = $219M 2022: quarterly hike $0.01, cumulative $0.04 = $292M 2023: quarterly hike $0.01, cumulative $0.05 = $365M Based on simple annual quarterly dividend hikes of $0.01, AT&T would be obligated to pay an additional $365 million in quarterly dividend payouts. The annual obligation total grows almost $1.5 billion by 2023.
The annual hikes will start falling far below 2% so investors shouldn't be surprised with more than a $0.01 hike by 2023 to keep investors happy. AT&T already would be responsible for annual dividend payouts of $16 billion.
Even if AT&T reaches their debt reduction goal of $150 billion at the end of 2019, the wireless giant is left with a massive debt balance and more than $20 billion in annual capital expenditures. The last thing the company needs are these large and growing dividend requirements as a financial noose.
The big issue with AT&T entering the media space is the potential competition like Alphabet ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) and Apple ( AAPL ) have cash balances in excess of $100 billion without crushing dividend payout requirements. This chart doesn't accurately reflect the net cash position of Apple, but the stark differences in the balance sheets of these companies places AT&T at a huge competitive disadvantage.
T Net Total Long Term Debt (Quarterly) data by YCharts Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that investors shouldn't actually celebrate dividend hikes that obligate AT&T to larger dividend payouts. The company has better uses of corporate cash than additional payouts to shareholders that aren't actually rewarded by these distributions due to the stock weakness.
The stock is a bargain at $30, but investors aren't actually better off by these larger dividend obligations while forced to unload an asset like Hulu to effectively pay these larger dividends.
